items.stem: In the example of an athlete running back and forth on a straight track as shown in the figure , when will the displacement of the athlete be zero? What will be the total distance travelled in that case?
items.answer: The displacement of the athlete will be zero when they return to their initial starting point O. In this case, since the athlete ran from point O to point A (100 m) and then all the way back to point O (100 m), the total distance travelled will be 200 m.

items.stem: Fuel used up in a vehicle depends on which of the following? Justify your answer. (i) Total distance travelled (ii) Displacement
items.answer: Fuel used up in a vehicle depends on the (i) total distance travelled. This is because the engine must continuously burn fuel to generate energy for every part of the physical path the vehicle moves along, regardless of its direction. Even if a vehicle returns to its starting point resulting in a net displacement of zero, fuel has been constantly consumed throughout the journey to cover the actual distance driven.

items.stem: A ball rolls down an inclined track as shown in Figure Is its motion, a straight line motion? Assuming the starting point of the ball (O) to be the origin, can its motion from O to D be depicted using a horizontal line as shown in Figure? Are the values of total distance travelled and magnitude of displacement from O equal or different at positions A, B, C and D?
items.answer: Yes, the motion of the ball rolling down the inclined track is a straight line motion because it follows a single linear path downwards. Assuming the starting point O is the origin, its motion can easily be depicted using a horizontal line by simply defining the positive direction along the track and mapping the linear measurements to a straight horizontal axis. Furthermore, because the ball continuously moves in only one forward direction without turning back, the values of total distance travelled and the magnitude of displacement from O will be exactly equal at all positions A, B, C, and D.

items.stem: During a family road trip, you drive 200 km north in three hours. Afterwards, you drive 200 km south in two hours. Find the average speed and average velocity for your entire trip.
items.answer: Leg Direction Distance Displacement Time Leg 1 North (+) 200 km +200 km 3 h Leg 2 South (−) 200 km −200 km 2 h Total — 400 km 0 km 5 h Average Speed = Total Distance ÷ Total Time = 400 km ÷ 5 h Average Speed = 80 km/h Average Velocity = Total Displacement ÷ Total Time = (+200) + (−200) ÷ 5 h = 0 km ÷ 5 h Average Velocity = 0 km/h

items.stem: Under what condition(s) is the (i) magnitude of average velocity of an object equal to its average speed? (ii) magnitude of average velocity of an object zero while its average speed is not zero?
items.answer: (i) The magnitude of average velocity is equal to average speed only when an object moves in a straight line in a single direction without ever turning back, ensuring that the total distance travelled perfectly equals the magnitude of displacement. (ii) The average velocity is zero while the average speed is not zero when an object completes a journey where its final position is the same as its starting position. In this scenario, the overall displacement is zero, but the object has still covered a measurable total distance during its movement. NCER T Exercis

items.stem: My father went to a shop from home which is located at a distance of 250 m on a straight road. On reaching there, he discovered that he forgot to carry a cloth bag. He came home to take it, went to the shop again, bought provisions and came back home. How much was the total distance travelled by him? What was his displacement from home?
items.answer: The total distance travelled is the sum of all the path lengths covered. He went to the shop (250 m), came back home (250 m), went to the shop again (250 m), and finally came back home (250 m). Total distance = 250 + 250 + 250 + 250 = 1000 m. Since his initial position (home) and final position (home) are the same, the net change in his position is zero. Therefore, his displacement from home is 0 m.

items.stem: A student runs from the ground floor to the fourth floor of a school building to collect a book and then comes down to their classroom on the second floor. If the height of each floor is 3 m, find: (i) the total vertical distance travelled, and (ii) their displacement from the starting point.
items.answer: (i) The student travels up 4 floors (ground to 4th) and then down 2 floors (4th to 2nd). Total floors covered = 4 + 2 = 6 floors. Total vertical distance travelled = 6 floors x 3 m/floor = 18 m. (ii) Displacement is the shortest straight- line distance between the initial and final positions. The starting point is the ground floor (0 m) and the final point is the second floor (2 floors × 3 m = 6 m high). Therefore, the displacement is 6 m upwards from the starting point.

items.stem: A girl is riding her scooter and finds that its speedometer reading is constant. Is it possible for her scooter to be accelerating and if so, how?
items.answer: Yes, it is possible for the scooter to be accelerating even if the speedometer reading (which measures only speed) is constant. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, and velocity has both magnitude (speed) and direction. If the girl is riding her scooter along a circular or curved path at a constant speed, the direction of her motion is continuously changing. This continuous change in direction means her velocity is changing, which results in the scooter accelerating. Describing Motion Around Us

items.stem: Figure shows a position-time graph of two objects A and B that are moving along the parallel tracks in the same direction. Do objects A and B ever have equal velocity? Justify your answer.
items.answer: Based on the position-time graph in figure , objects A and B do not ever have equal velocity. The velocity of an object is given by the slope of its position-time graph. Since the graphs for both objects are straight lines, they are moving with constant velocities. However, the line for object A is steeper than the line for object B, indicating that the slope of A is greater than the slope of B. Because their slopes (velocities) are constant and different from each other throughout the motion, they never have equal velocity.

items.stem: A graph in figure shows the change in position with time for two objects A and B moving in a straight line from 0 to 10 seconds. Choose the correct option(s). (i) The average velocity of both over the 10 s time interval is equal since they have the same initial and final positions. (ii) The average speeds of both over the 10 s time interval are equal since both cover equal distance in equal time. (iii) The average speed of A over the 10 s time interval is lower than that of B since it covers a shorter distance than B in 10 seconds. (iv) The average speed of A over the 10 s time interval is greater than that of B since B’s speed is lower than A’s in some segments.
items.answer: The correct options are (i) and (ii). According to the graph, both objects start at position 0 at time 0 s and end at the exact same position at time 10 s. Since their initial and final positions are identical, their net displacements are equal. Dividing this equal displacement by the same 10 s time interval gives equal average velocities, confirming option (i). Furthermore, because both objects move in a straight line in one direction without turning back (position only increases), their total distance travelled is equal to the magnitude of their displacement. Since both covered equal total distance in the same time, their average speeds are also equal, confirming option (ii).

items.stem: A student said, “The Earth moves around the Sun”. In this context, discuss whether an object kept on the Earth can be considered to be at rest.
items.answer: Motion is a relative concept, meaning whether an object is at rest or in motion depends on the observer’s frame of reference. An object kept on the Earth is at rest with respect to the Earth itself, because its position relative to the Earth’s surface does not change with time. However, if that same object is observed from the perspective of the Sun or from space, it is in continuous motion because it revolves around the Sun along with the Earth. Therefore, the object can be considered at rest relative to the Earth, but it is simultaneously in motion relative to the Sun.

items.stem: A girl is preparing for her first marathon by running on a straight road. She uses a smart watch to calculate her running speed at different intervals. The graph depicts her velocity versus time. Estimate the running distance based on the Click Here to Buy book on Amazon graph.
items.answer: Reading the Graph Phase Time interval Velocity Motion I 0 – 1 h 0 → 7.5 km h⁻¹ Increasing II 1 – 5 h 7.5 km h⁻¹ (constant) Constant velocity III 5 – 6 h 7.5 → 5 km h⁻¹ Decreasing Distance = Area under the v – t graph. Each phase is treated as a standard geometric shape. Phase I (0 – 1 h) — Area of triangle s1 = 2 1 × base × height = 2 1 × 1 × 7.5 = 3.75 km Phase II (1 – 5 h) — Area of rectangle s2 = v × t = 7.5 × 4 = 30 km Phase III (5 – 6 h) — Area of trapezium s3 = 2 1 × (u + v) × t = 2 1 × (7.5 + 5) × 1 = 2 1 × 12.5 × 1 = 6.25 km Total Distance S = s1 + s2 + s3 = 3.75 + 30 + 6.25 = 40 km

items.stem: On entering a state highway, a car continues to move with a constant velocity of 6 m s-1 for 2 minutes and then accelerates with a constant acceleration 1 m s-2 for 6 seconds. Find the displacement of the car on the state highway in the 2 min 6 s time interval by drawing a velocity- time graph for its motion.
